problem: Existing zero-shot ObjectNav methods (VLFM, ApexNav, etc.) use one object-agnostic strategy and do not adapt the weight of room-level versus object-level contextual cues to the target. Online-LLM methods add latency and compute overhead.
motivation: Some targets (toilet) are tightly tied to a room type, while others (chair, TV, potted plant) are better found via co-located objects. Ignoring this makes exploration inefficient and inaccurate. Offline LLM queries can supply commonsense without runtime cost for on-board robots.
key_idea: Build a unified semantic value map that fuses target, contextual-room and contextual-object scores, weighted by the normalized entropy of the LLM-estimated target-room association distribution (low entropy favors room cues, high entropy favors object cues).
insight: Adaptive entropy weighting beats fixed weights: overall SR is 61.7 vs 59.8 (room-only), 60.2 (equal) and 61.2 (object-only). Per-target results show room-only is good for low-entropy targets (toilet) but hurts high-entropy ones (chair 69.0 vs 73.3; potted plant 38.1 vs 42.9). Adding both context types gives 61.2 SR / 33.8 SPL against 59.6 / 33.0 without them. Gains are modest (about 2 SR over ApexNav), and the fixed-weight variants are close to the adaptive one.
method: Target object score: BLIP2 cosine similarity between view and target category, as in VLFM. The value map is updated by a confidence-weighted average with cos² FoV-based confidence.
Contextual room score: same BLIP2 pipeline, but the text prompt is the LLM-identified most likely room type, giving a global cue.

Contextual object score: the offline LLM lists co-located objects and correlations cor(target, obj). Detected objects (YOLOv7 / GroundingDINO + MobileSAM) put a Gaussian on the 2D map, with amplitude A0·cor and sigma σ0+cor.
Entropy-based fusion: the LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) gives P(room|target). Normalized entropy H yields v_sem = v_target + (1-H)·v_room + H·v_object.

Exploration: initial in-place rotation, then a conditional ApexNav-style strategy. TSP geometry-based exploration runs until a frontier's semantic score passes a threshold, then the highest-scoring frontier is selected.
Multi-view verification: the agent visits several viewpoints around a candidate and aggregates detection count and class agreement to reject false positives.

setting.backbone: BLIP2 (frozen) for value maps; Gemini-Pro 2.5 (frozen, offline queries); YOLOv7 / GroundingDINO detectors; MobileSAM
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D 640x480 (depth 0.5-5 m) with pose; real robot uses LiDAR + omnidirectional camera
setting.action_space: discrete: forward 0.2 m / turn 30°, with frontier-based waypoint planning

numbers.extra: offline LLM queries only; T=500 steps, success distance 0.2 m
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Performance comparison on HM3D benchmark, CLUE (Ours) 61.7 / 34.3

numbers_note: Only HM3D reported (2000 episodes, 20 scenes, 6 categories); split labelled 'validation set' in text. Resource analysis is in a figure only.
results: CLUE reaches 61.7 SR / 34.3 SPL on HM3D, beating ApexNav (59.6 / 33.0), the strongest baseline, and all online-LLM methods (best TriHelper 56.5 SR / 25.3 SPL). It also uses fewer resources and less time than SG-Nav, and worked in real-world Jackal tests.
limitations: Assumes predefined room categories and precomputed LLM knowledge, which limits open-set generalization
Improvement over ApexNav is modest (about 2 SR), the real-world evaluation is qualitative only with no quantitative results, and the paper says HM3D val 'used 2000 episodes'
Hand-set entropy-to-weight mapping is linear and heuristic, and does not always beat the best fixed weights per object
